planting.note: Direct sow once soil has fully warmed; because this landrace matures so late, gardeners in short-season climates should give it the earliest safe start.

directions: Seoritae, whose name literally means 'frost soybean,' is a traditional Korean black-seeded landrace deliberately left standing in the field until after the first light autumn frost, a practice believed to sweeten the bean and deepen the anthocyanin pigment in its glossy black seed coat. Home cooks simmer the beans whole into kongbap rice, roast them for snacking, or press them into a dark, nutty soy milk. Because it is one of the latest-maturing soybean types grown in Korea, gardeners outside its native long, warm growing season should start it at the earliest safe date after the last frost. Harvest once pods are dry and rattle and the foliage has yellowed and dropped.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed; compact bushy plants tolerate closer spacing than larger-seeded soybean landraces.

directions: Jwinuni-kong takes its name, literally 'rat's-eye bean,' from its small, glossy, jet-black seed, noticeably smaller than standard black soybean types like seoritae. Traditional Korean households simmer the dried beans whole in soy sauce as a side dish called kongjang or boil them into a dark tonic drink, yakkong, long believed to support digestion and liver health. The compact, bushy plants tolerate closer in-row spacing than larger-seeded soybean landraces and are easy to grow in a home garden. Harvest once pods are fully dry and rattle, then thresh and store the beans in a cool, dry place.

common_name: Baektae Soybean (Korean White Soybean for Doenjang & Tofu)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed, as for any bush soybean.

directions: Baektae is the pale yellow-seeded soybean landrace that forms the everyday backbone of Korean fermentation, ground and boiled down into doenjang (soybean paste), ganjang (soy sauce), and fresh tubu (tofu). Its mild, starchy seed sets it apart from dark-seeded eating types like seoritae and jwinuni-kong, which Korean cooks reserve mainly for simmered or roasted bean dishes rather than fermentation. Grow it exactly as you would any warm-season bush soybean, direct-sown once the soil has warmed, and harvest the pods dry once the leaves have dropped and the pods rattle with mature seed. Save a portion of clean, fully dry seed to inoculate the next batch of homemade meju starter.

planting.note: Transplant nursery-raised seedlings into deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil under filtered high shade once all frost risk has passed.

directions: Wolisho is one of the named Ethiopian landrace types long maintained by farmers in the forested highlands around Yirgacheffe and the wider Gedeo growing zone, distinct from the generic unselected seed mix most 'Ethiopian heirloom' coffee is grown from. Like other Ethiopian landraces, it carries far more internal genetic diversity than a single modern clone, yielding cherries with the floral, citrusy cup character the region is known for. Grow it under the dappled high shade of a forest-garden canopy with steady moisture and rich, slightly acidic soil, mirroring its native highland habitat. Expect only a light first harvest after three to four years, with yields building over subsequent seasons.
sources: World Coffee Research — Arabica Coffee Varieties catalog

planting.note: Transplant nursery-raised seedlings into deep, friable, humus-rich soil under high filtered shade once all frost risk has passed.

directions: Kurume is a tall, vigorous Ethiopian landrace type kept within the country's large pool of named local coffee selections, traditionally grown as part of a shaded forest-garden system rather than planted as a single clonal variety. Its name distinguishes it from other locally recognized landraces such as Wolisho, each shaped informally over generations by farmers selecting for traits like vigor, bean size, or local hardiness rather than through a formal breeding program. Give it the same deep, friable, humus-rich soil and high filtered shade that Ethiopian coffee receives in its native highland forest gardens, with mulch to keep roots cool and moist. As with other Coffea arabica trees, patience is required: the first meaningful cherry harvest typically arrives three to four years after transplanting.
sources: World Coffee Research — Arabica Coffee Varieties catalog
